world_behind.title: The morning after
world_behind.text: Jacob closed the previous day by promising the remainder of his words, and this is that remainder. Between the two sessions an angel visited him, which he mentions in passing while making a different point. The colony heard the plan of salvation one day and the future of their land and children the next.

world_behind.title: A name arrives
world_behind.text: Verse 3 records the moment the title the record will use thousands of times is first given: "for in the last night the angel spake unto me that this should be his name" (v. 3). Before this the record's writers say Messiah, Redeemer, Lamb of God, Holy One of Israel. The Greek-derived name enters through an angel and through Jacob, not through a translator's preference.

cites.quote: for in the last night the angel spake unto me that this should be his name

spans.text: for in the last night the angel spake unto me that this should be his name

world_behind.title: Jerusalem's verdict, spoken by an exile
world_behind.text: Jacob says the crucifixion will happen there because no other nation would do it, which is a hard thing for a man whose family fled that city. His father had preached against it and been driven out; the judgment in verses 3 through 6 is a second-generation restatement of the grievance that started the migration.

world_behind.title: What "this land" meant to the hearers
world_behind.text: The land promises of verses 10 through 19 concern a place the colony had lived in for a few decades at most. They had no cities to speak of and one temple. The promises are spoken about a future the hearers cannot check, which is why the chapter's closing turn is toward what they can do about their own state.

world_behind.title: Gentile kings as caretakers
world_behind.text: Verse 9 borrows Isaiah's picture of foreign monarchs carrying Israel's children home. Under empire after empire this was the reverse of the family's experience of Gentile power. Jacob reads the reversal as covenant work rather than politics, and verse 18 admits the affliction that comes first.

world_behind.title: Islands, and the word for them
world_behind.text: Verse 21 draws a conclusion from a plural: since the prophets said isles, there must be more than this one, and other broken-off branches live on them. It is a small piece of reasoning from the text itself, and it tells us something about how this colony read scripture, closely, and for information about themselves.

words.text: The name appears here for the first time in the record, delivered by an angel the night before the sermon. Jacob inserts the fact as an aside inside a sentence about the crucifixion, then uses the name again four verses later as the content of belief: "that I am Christ" (v. 7). What the record had been circling with titles now has a name to be believed in, and the chapters that follow use it freely.

Jacob's coinage as far as the record goes, and he leaves it undefined, trusting his hearers to hear the two halves: priest work done as a craft, for pay. Nephi will define it later as men setting themselves up for a light and getting gain. Here it is named as one of the two causes of the crucifixion, which puts professional religion beside plain iniquity in the same sentence.

A scattering word with a long tail: not exile to one place but distribution across many. Jacob pairs it with "long" (v. 8), giving the scattering a duration rather than only an extent. For hearers who were themselves a fragment carried off the map, the word describes their own situation and promises its end in the same clause.

Military engineering: walls, ditches, ramparts. Nephi's people were building defenses in this period, so the verb landed as a description of work they knew. God claims the job for himself over the whole land, and the sentence is one line long with no conditions attached to it, which is unusual in a chapter full of conditions.

A counting word used for belonging. Gentiles who come into the covenant are "numbered among the house of Israel" (v. 18), and the land is consecrated to Jacob's seed "and them who shall be numbered among thy seed" (v. 19). Membership in this chapter is a matter of being counted in a list rather than of descent, which is a striking thing to say to a family that had been keeping careful track of its own lineage.

cites.quote: numbered among the house of Israel

spans.text: numbered among the house of Israel

cites.quote: and them who shall be numbered among thy seed

spans.text: and them who shall be numbered among thy seed

words.text: The last word of the sermon, and it sits after its noun: "praise him through grace divine" (v. 25). English usually puts the adjective first, and the inversion has the feel of a translated Hebrew phrase where the modifier follows. Whatever its source, the word order slows the sentence down at the end of five chapters and leaves the hearers on the attribute rather than on the gift.

phrases.term: the angel spake unto me that this should be his name
phrases.text: A revelation reported as a parenthesis. Jacob is mid-sentence about what must happen among the Jews, and the name arrives inside a pair of dashes as though it were a clarification rather than the news it is. The casualness is worth noticing: the colony's preacher receives the name of God the night before he needs it, and mentions it the way a man mentions the source of a quotation.

phrases.term: none other nation on earth that would crucify their God
phrases.text: The chapter's hardest sentence, and it is an argument about privilege, not race. Verse 4 supplies the reasoning: miracles among other nations would produce repentance, so only a people who had already seen and heard the most could reject the most. The logic indicts by way of advantage, and it is the same logic Jacob turned on his own congregation the day before when he said the wo falls on those who have the law "like unto us" (9:27).

phrases.term: the kings of the Gentiles shall be nursing fathers
phrases.text: Jacob read this line aloud from Isaiah two chapters earlier, when "kings shall be thy nursing fathers" (6:7) came in the middle of the quoted block. Now he restates it in his own voice with a change: Isaiah's kings become "the kings of the Gentiles" (v. 9), and the bowing down is dropped. The reading has become an application, which is what he promised in chapter 6 that he would do.

Lehi's phrase from his deathbed blessing, where the land was promised as "a land of liberty unto them" (2 Ne. 1:7) if its people served God. Jacob puts the same words in God's mouth and directs them at the Gentiles who will one day hold the land. Between father and son the promise widens from the family's inheritance to a condition of the place itself.

phrases.term: he that fighteth against Zion shall perish
phrases.text: Said twice, three verses apart, the second time with a list attached: Jew and Gentile, bond and free, male and female. Nephi had already written that "all that fight against Zion shall be destroyed" (1 Ne. 22:14). The doubling here is not repetition for emphasis. The first is a rule; the second removes every category anyone might have hoped to be exempt in.

phrases.term: the whore of all the earth
phrases.text: Nephi used the figure in his vision for the great church that fights the saints; Jacob applies it to a behavior rather than an institution. Whoever fights Zion, of any nation or station, is the whore of all the earth. The move is characteristic of this sermon: categories his brother saw as bodies, Jacob turns into descriptions of what people do.

Three days of preaching converge on this clause. The reading Jacob delivered opened with God asking whether he had cast Israel off and demanding the divorce papers (7:1). Here is the answer, applied to the people in front of him, and it is given as a reason not to hang down their heads. The exiles' oldest fear is retired in five words.

phrases.term: we are upon an isle of the sea
phrases.text: The record's first plain statement of where these people actually are. Jacob offers it as consolation, not geography: driven out of one land, led to a better one, with the sea as the road rather than the obstacle. Everything the family suffered on the water is recategorized in a single sentence as transport.

phrases.term: ye are free to act for yourselves
phrases.text: Lehi told his sons they were "free to choose liberty and eternal life" (2 Ne. 2:27). Jacob shortens it and changes the verb from choosing to acting, then restores the two roads immediately. Placed after fifteen verses of prophecy about nations, the sentence hands the initiative back to individuals who have just been told their future is largely out of their hands.

phrases.term: reconcile yourselves to the will of God
phrases.text: The verb assumes the estrangement is real and puts the moving on the human side. Paul's version asks his readers to "be ye reconciled to God" (2 Cor. 5:20), passive; Jacob's is reflexive, something a person does to himself. His own son-in-the-faith language later returns to the idea, and the chapter's next clause makes sure the reflexive verb is not mistaken for self-rescue.

phrases.term: only in and through the grace of God that ye are saved
phrases.text: The qualifier arrives immediately after the command, and the word "only" does the work. Reconciling is something the hearer performs; being saved is not. Paul's "by grace are ye saved through faith" (Eph. 2:8) says the same in fewer words. Jacob's addition is the sequence: he tells them to act first and then tells them the acting was never the mechanism.

verses.label: v. 1–3
verses.title: A branch, and a name
verses.text: The sermon resumes on the word it paused on, the righteous branch, and within two verses delivers the name of Christ. The order matters. The promise about descendants comes first, and the name arrives as the thing that will one day give those descendants "the true knowledge of their Redeemer" (v. 2). Even the chapter's most famous disclosure is in service of the covenant argument around it.

cites.quote: the true knowledge of their Redeemer

spans.text: the true knowledge of their Redeemer

verses.label: v. 4–6
verses.title: The argument from advantage
verses.text: Three verses explain why the crucifixion happens where it does, and the reasoning is uncomfortable by design: greater light makes greater rejection possible. Then the consequences are listed without commentary, destruction and scattering. Jacob does not soften the verdict, and he does not gloat over it either; the next verse begins the restoration.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: The terms of coming home
verses.text: Belief is the trigger, "that I am Christ" (v. 7), and the covenant with the fathers is the ground. What follows is logistics: gathered from the isles and the four parts of the earth, carried by Gentile kings. The passage answers a question the colony had to be asking, whether being far away had disqualified them, and the answer is that distance is a transport problem.

verses.label: v. 11–14
verses.title: A land with one king
verses.text: Four short verses set the political terms of the promised land: liberty, no kings raised up, fortification, and the reason under all three, "I, the Lord, the king of heaven, will be their king" (v. 14). Nephi had already refused the crown his people offered him. The chapter turns his personal refusal into a standing condition of the land itself.

cites.quote: I, the Lord, the king of heaven, will be their king

spans.text: I, the Lord, the king of heaven, will be their king

verses.label: v. 16
verses.title: No exemptions
verses.text: The verse takes the rule of verse 13 and closes every gap in it, then adds the sharpest line of the chapter: "they who are not for me are against me" (v. 16). Neutrality is removed as an option in the same breath that removes nationality, status, and sex. For a small colony with its own factions, the verse leaves no seat in the middle of the room.

cites.quote: they who are not for me are against me

spans.text: they who are not for me are against me

verses.label: v. 20–22
verses.title: Broken off, and remembered
verses.text: The comfort widens in three steps. First this colony, led to a better land; then every island the prophets mentioned, inhabited by brethren nobody here has met; then all who have been broken off from the house of Israel at any time. Only after that scope is set does Jacob bring it home: "he remembereth us also" (v. 22). Consolation in this sermon works by enlargement rather than by focus.

verses.label: v. 23–25
verses.title: Cheer up, choose, be reconciled
verses.text: The close moves fast through four imperatives and ends on a blessing rather than a warning. Jacob asks for cheerful hearts from people he spent a day frightening, and the request is not inconsistent: the fear was aimed at what they could change, and the cheer rests on what they cannot. The last verse asks God to raise them by resurrection and by atonement, the two powers his long sermon explained.

chapter.title: Day two answers day one
chapter.text: The previous chapter argued the plan and named the ways to waste it; this one tells the same hearers they are not cast off, their children will be restored, and they may cheer up. A sermon that ended at chapter 9 would be a warning. The pair is a pastoral sequence, and the order is deliberate.

chapter.title: The chapter converts reading into application
chapter.text: Jacob promised in chapter 6 that Isaiah's words could be likened to his hearers. Here he does it in the open: the nursing fathers become the Gentile kings who will carry his descendants, and the isles of the prophets become the island the colony is standing on. The method the record keeps recommending gets a full demonstration.

chapter.title: Geography becomes doctrine
chapter.text: Land, liberty, kingship, and fortification are treated as covenant terms rather than circumstances. The most consequential move is verse 14's, which makes the absence of a king on this land a statement about who the king is. Later politics in the record, especially the end of Nephite monarchy, argue from ground this chapter lays.

chapter.title: Both halves of the Gentile picture are kept
chapter.text: Verse 18 says the Gentiles will afflict Jacob's seed; verses 9 and 10 say Gentile kings will nurse and be blessed. The chapter refuses to simplify in either direction, and it never resolves the tension into a single verdict on outsiders. That restraint is unusual in a text written by people who had reason to hold a grudge.

chapter.title: The sermon ends where the record's arguments about salvation will keep ending
chapter.text: Reconcile yourselves, and know that grace does the saving. Nephi will return to this pairing in his own words, and Jacob's own later sermons keep the same order of operations. The unit closes on the record's characteristic combination of demand and gift, stated compactly enough to be memorized.

chapter.title: A first name given in an aside
chapter.text: The record's most-used name for God arrives inside a subordinate clause. Nothing in the chapter's structure marks the moment, and Jacob preaches on past it without pausing. Readers who know how often the name will be used afterward feel the weight; the sermon's own hearers were given it and immediately told what to do with it.

chapter.title: The unit's closing panel
chapter.text: Chapters 6 through 10 move from quoted prophecy to explained doctrine to applied covenant. This chapter is the panel that lands everything on the hearers' own island, their own children, their own choice, and Nephi resumes the record in the next chapter with his own reasons for loving the words of Isaiah.

applications.title: Separate history from verdict
applications.text: Write down the hardest thing that has happened to you, then write separately what you have concluded about God's view of you from it. Jacob's hearers had been driven out; they had not been cast off. Most despair lives in the gap between the two sentences.

applications.title: Check what your advantages obligate
applications.text: The chapter's uncomfortable logic is that greater light raises the stakes of rejecting it. Inventory what you have been given, access, teaching, time, and name the one place where you know more than you are currently living. Advantage is not a comfort in this chapter.

applications.title: Read a plural closely
applications.text: Jacob built a doctrine out of the fact that the prophets said isles rather than isle. Take one verse you think you know and read it slowly enough to notice a number, a tense, or a preposition you had passed over. The habit this chapter models is attention, not cleverness.

applications.title: Name your king
applications.text: The land has no king because God is the king. Ask what actually functions as final authority in a given area of your life, the calendar, the client, the crowd, and consider what would change in that area if the answer in verse 14 were operative.

applications.title: Do the reflexive work
applications.text: Reconciling is something you do to yourself, not something you wait to feel. Pick the one place you are estranged from what God has asked, and take the first concrete step toward it this week without waiting for the desire to arrive first.

applications.title: Then stop counting
applications.text: After you have acted, practice saying the second half of the verse out loud about your own case: it is only in and through grace that I am saved. The order in the verse is the order in the week. The acting comes first and explains nothing.

applications.title: Cheer up on purpose
applications.text: Jacob commands cheerfulness to people who have just been told about the whore of all the earth. Find the specific promise in your own life that would justify a lighter heart, say it plainly, and let it change one thing about how you carry yourself today.

questions.text: What difference does it make to me that a name I use daily was given to somebody, at night, and written down?
Where do I do religious work as a craft, for something other than what it is for?
In what specific way have I recently been fighting against Zion rather than for it, in a room, a thread, or a family?
Where am I trying to hold a neutral position that this verse says does not exist?
Which of my losses have I quietly read as evidence of being cast off, and what would it take to reclassify it?
If I am free to act, what am I waiting for permission or feeling to do?
What would reconciling myself to God's will look like this week, in one concrete act rather than an attitude?
